endorsements.quote: Hence, we recommend that AI development teams should involve all relevant stakeholders at all stages of the AI life cycle, that is, conception, technical development, clinical validation, and real-world deployment ( Textbox 1 ).

Depending on the AI application, a range of health care professionals, such as general practitioners, specialists (domain experts), health care managers, nurses, and technicians, should be engaged for requirements elicitation.
Including vulnerable groups and minorities in AI design and development can help develop tools that are respectful of diverse needs and contexts.

Ethicists and social scientists should also play a crucial role during conception, especially for anticipating the application-specific ethical and social impacts of the AI tools, such as misalignments with fundamental rights, effects on deskilling, changes in power relationships, and alterations in human behaviors as AI is integrated into care settings.

This includes compiling diverse and representative training datasets, employing machine learning methods that minimize potential biases, and developing AI-human interfaces that enhance user interaction and comprehension of the AI system.

This includes conducting periodic evaluations and audits to identify any performance degradation or emerging ethical issues, implementing logging systems to enhance traceability and accountability, and ensuring robust human oversight mechanisms are in place.
Doctors should be informed of these limitations during training and should be alerted when the system is used in these cases.

For instance, in the clinical context, it was deemed essential to know how the AI tool was built, eg, the type of dataset that was used to train the algorithm, its limitations and biases, the accuracy of the performance, but also the uncertainty of the outcome.

This should include that AI systems communicate their limitations, for example, their inability to provide an accurate answer for a given patient or, in general, having a greater accuracy for certain patient groups, as well as include proper uncertainty quantification for their results [ 73 ].
User-oriented knowledge takes several information needs of different stakeholders into account, such as developers, users, and patients, and these vary.
The additional training for medical professionals in the use of AI should include methods for quick and reliable assessment of tools in daily practice.

unlisted_practices: Include alert systems in medical AI tools to warn users when cases fall out of scope or outside the tool's intended use.
Involve physicians in a human-in-the-loop manner during AI tool development and testing.
Keep AI training limited in attention and time consumption while sufficient for safe use, and integrate AI tools seamlessly into clinical workflows.
Involve professional associations as institutional stakeholders in developing AI training materials.
Ensure AI screening tools achieve sensitivity at least matching the average sensitivity of radiologists in national screening programs.
Involve social scientists in validation to evaluate socio-behavioral effects of AI on users, including trust, retained judgment, and doctor-patient relationships.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint article presenting conceptual analysis and recommendations from an interdisciplinary expert workshop on trust and trustworthy AI in medicine.
